source_text: ΠΕΡΙ ΤΗΣ ΤΩΝ ΝΕΚΡΩΝ ΑΝΑΣΤΑΣΕΩΣ ΟΜΙΛΙΑ αʹ. Περὶ δογμάτων ὑμῖν ἔμπροσθεν διελέχθημεν καὶ τῆς τοῦ μονογενοῦς Υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ δόξης, ἐπιστομίζοντες τοὺς καθαιροῦντας αὐτοῦ τὴν ἀξίαν, καὶ τοῦ γεγεννηκότος αὐτὸν ἀλλοτριοῦντας· σήμερον τὸν ἠθικώτερον βούλομαι γυμνάσαι λόγον, καὶ περὶ βίου καὶ πολιτείας ἅπασαν ποιήσασθαι τὴν παραίνεσιν· μᾶλλον δὲ οὐκ ἠθικὸς ἔσται μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ δογματικὸς οὗτος ὁ λόγος· εἰς γὰρ τὴν περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ὑπόθεσιν καθεῖναι παρασκευάζομαι. Αὕτη δὲ ἡ ὑπόθεσις ποικίλη τίς ἐστιν, ὁμοῦ καὶ εἰς δόγματα ἡμᾶς διορθοῦσα, καὶ τὸν βίον ἡμῶν ῥυθμίζουσα, καὶ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόνοιαν ἁπάσης ἀπαλλάττουσα κατηγορίας. Καὶ ὥσπερ ἀπιστουμένη, τὴν ζωὴν ἀνατρέπει τὴν ἡμετέραν, καὶ μυρίων κακῶν ἐμπίπλησι, καὶ τὰ ἄνω κάτω ποιεῖ· οὕτω πιστευομένη, τοὺς περὶ τῆς Προνοίας ἡμῖν συνεισάγει λόγους, καὶ πολλὴν τῆς ἀρετῆς παρασκευάζει ποιεῖσθαι τὴν ἐπιμέλειαν, καὶ μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς σπουδῆς τὴν κακίαν φεύγειν, καὶ γαλήνης ἅπαντα καὶ εἰρήνης πληροῖ. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ μὴ προσδοκῶν ἀναστήσεσθαι, μηδὲ εὐθύνας δώσειν τῶν ἐνταῦθα πεπραγμένων αὐτῷ, ἀλλὰ μέχρι τοῦ παρόντος βίου τὰ ἡμέτερα στήσεσθαι νομίζων, καὶ περαιτέρω μηδὲν εἶναι πλέον, οὔτε ἀρετῆς ἐπιμελήσεται· πῶς γὰρ, μηδεμίαν προσδοκῶν ἀμοιβὴν αὐτῷ κεῖσθαι τῶν πόνων; οὔτε κακίας ἀφέξεται, μηδεμίαν προσδοκῶν ὑποστήσεσθαι κόλασιν τῶν κακῶς αὐτῷ πεπραγμένων· ἀλλ' ἐπιδοὺς ἑαυτὸν ταῖς ἀτόποις ἐπιθυμίαις, πᾶν εἶδος ἐπελεύσεται πονηρίας. Ὁ δὲ περὶ τῆς μελλούσης πεπεικὼς ἑαυτὸν κρίσεως, καὶ τὸ φοβερὸν δικαστήριον ἐκεῖνο πρὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἔχων, καὶ τὰς ἀπαραιτήτους εὐθύνας καὶ τὴν ἀπαραλόγιστον ψῆφον, παντὶ τρόπῳ πειράσεται σωφροσύνης μὲν καὶ ἐπιεικείας ἀντέχεσθαι καὶ τῆς ἄλλης ἀρετῆς, ἀκολασίαν δὲ καὶ θρασύτητα καὶ τὴν ἄλλην ἅπασαν πονηρίαν φεύγειν· καὶ τοὺς κατηγοροῦντας δὲ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ προνοίας μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας ἐντεῦθεν ἐπιστομίσαι οὗτος δυνήσεται. Ὅταν γὰρ ὁρῶντές τινες τοὺς μὲν ἐπιεικεῖς καὶ σώφρονας καὶ ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ζῶντας, ἀγχομένους ὑπὸ πενίας, ἐπηρεαζομένους, συκοφαντουμένους, μόλις τῆς ἀναγκαίας εὐποροῦντας τροφῆς, πολλάκις δὲ καὶ νόσῳ μακρᾷ καὶ χαλεποῖς νοσήμασι ταριχευομένους, καὶ οὐδεμιᾶς τυγχάνοντας προστασίας, ἀνθρώπους δὲ γόητας καὶ μιαροὺς καὶ πολλῶν γέμοντας κακῶν πλοῦτον περιβεβλημένους, τρυφῶντας, λαμπρὰ περικειμένους ἱμάτια, ἐσμὸν οἰκετῶν ἐπισυρομένους πολὺν, θαυμαζομένους, δυναστείας ἀπολαύοντας, παρὰ βασιλεῖ πολλὴν κεκτημένους παῤῥησίαν· εἶτά τινες ὑπὲρ τούτων κατηγορῶσι τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ προνοίας, καὶ λέγωσι· Ποῦ ταῦτα προνοίας; ποῦ δὲ δικαίας κρίσεως; ὁ σώφρων καὶ ἐπιεικὴς ἐν κακοῖς, ὁ ἀκόλαστος καὶ διεφθαρμένος ἐν ἀγαθοῖς· καὶ οὗτος μὲν θαυμάζεται, ἐκεῖνος δὲ καταφρονεῖται· οὗτος ἀπολαύει τρυφῆς πολλῆς, ἐκεῖνος ἐν πενίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ἐσχάτοις ἐστὶ κακοῖς· ὁ μὲν περὶ τῶν μελλόντων ἀμφιβάλλων σιωπηθήσεται, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅλως ἐρεῖ· ὁ δὲ περὶ ἀναστάσεως φιλοσοφεῖν εἰδὼς, ῥᾳδίως τὴν βλασφημίαν ἐφέξει, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα ἀποδυσπετοῦντας ἐρεῖ· Παύσασθε κατὰ τοῦ πεποιηκότος ὑμᾶς Θεοῦ τὴν γλῶτταν ἀκονῶντες τὴν ἑαυτῶν. Οὐ γὰρ μέχρι τοῦ παρόντος βίου τὰ ἡμέτερα ἕστηκε πράγματα, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἑτέραν ζωὴν ἐπειγόμεθα πολλῷ μακροτέραν, μᾶλλον δὲ πέρας οὐκ ἔχουσαν· κἀκεῖ πάντως ὁ μὲν πένης οὗτος καὶ μετὰ δικαιοσύνης ζῶν, τῶν πόνων τούτων λήψεται τὰς ἀμοιβὰς, ὁ δὲ ἀκόλαστος καὶ γόης, τῆς πονηρίας ταύτης καὶ τῆς ἀδίκου τρυφῆς δώσει τὴν δίκην.
thought_title: The resurrection as the ground of moral life and theodicy
orientation: Chrysostom opens the homily by announcing that he will now turn from doctrinal disputes about the Son's glory to a discourse on the resurrection, which he says corrects doctrine, orders life, and answers accusations against God's providence.
pass_a_gloss: On the resurrection of the dead, homily 1. About doctrines we discoursed with you before, and about the glory of the only-begotten Son of God, stopping the mouths of those who tear down his dignity and alienate him from the one who begot him; today I wish to exercise a more ethical discourse, and to make the whole exhortation about life and conduct; rather, this discourse will not be ethical only, but also doctrinal; for I am preparing to let myself down into the subject of the resurrection. This subject is of many kinds, at once correcting us in doctrines, and ordering our life, and freeing the providence of God from every accusation. And just as, when disbelieved, it overturns our life, and fills it with ten thousand evils, and turns things upside down; so, when believed, it introduces to us the arguments about providence, and prepares us to make much care of virtue, and to flee wickedness with much zeal, and fills all things with calm and peace. For the one who does not expect to rise again, nor to give account of the things done by him here, but thinks that our affairs will stand only until the present life, and that beyond there is nothing more, will not care for virtue; for how could he, expecting no reward to be laid up for him for his labors? Nor will he keep away from wickedness, expecting to undergo no punishment for the things badly done by him; but having given himself over to disordered desires, he will go after every form of evil. But the one who has persuaded himself about the coming judgment, and has that fearful tribunal before his eyes, and the inexorable accounts and the undeceived verdict, will try in every way to hold fast to self-control and gentleness and the rest of virtue, and to flee licentiousness and boldness and all the rest of wickedness; and this one will be able with great abundance to stop the mouths of those who accuse the providence of God. For when some people see the gentle and self-controlled and those living in righteousness being choked by poverty, being mistreated, being slandered, scarcely having enough of necessary food, and often being embalmed by long illness and harsh diseases, and obtaining no protection, but charlatans and defiled men and those full of many evils having wrapped themselves in wealth, living in luxury, wearing bright garments, dragging after themselves a great swarm of household slaves, being admired, enjoying positions of power, having acquired much confidence before the king; then some people accuse the providence of God over these things, and say: Where is providence in these things? Where is just judgment? The self-controlled and gentle man is in evils, the licentious and corrupted man is in good things; and this one is admired, but that one is despised; this one enjoys much luxury, that one is in poverty and in the last evils; the one who doubts about the things to come will be silenced, and will say nothing at all; but the one who knows how to philosophize about the resurrection will easily check the blasphemy, and will say to those who are vexed at such things: Stop sharpening your own tongue against the God who made you. For our affairs do not stand only until the present life, but we are hastening toward another life much longer, or rather having no end; and there certainly this poor man who also lives with righteousness will receive the rewards of these labors, but the licentious man and charlatan will pay the penalty for this wickedness and unjust luxury.

choices.why: The verb means literally to put something on or over the mouth; 'stopping the mouths of' preserves the vivid physical image of silencing opponents.
The verb means to let down or lower; Chrysostom uses it metaphorically of descending into a deep subject, and the middle voice suggests his own action.
The idiom 'to make the upper things lower' means to throw everything into confusion; the English idiom 'turns things upside down' captures the same sense.
The verb means to preserve a corpse by embalming; Chrysostom uses it hyperbolically of the righteous being slowly consumed by long illness, as if being prepared for burial while alive.
The adjective means 'not to be deceived or cheated'; applied to the divine verdict it means a judgment that cannot be evaded or tricked.
The verb means to whet or sharpen; the image of sharpening one's tongue against God is vivid and should be kept.

pass_b_english: We spoke to you earlier about doctrines and about the glory of the only-begotten Son of God, stopping the mouths of those who tear down His dignity and alienate Him from His begetter. Today I want to exercise a more ethical discourse and make my whole exhortation about life and conduct. Yet this discourse will not be ethical only; it will also be doctrinal, for I am preparing to enter upon the subject of the resurrection. This subject is rich and varied: it sets our doctrines straight, orders our life, and frees God's providence from every accusation. When the resurrection is disbelieved, it overturns our life, fills it with countless evils, and turns things upside down. But when it is believed, it brings with it the arguments about providence, makes us take great care for virtue, makes us flee wickedness with great zeal, and fills everything with calm and peace.

The person who does not expect to rise again, who does not expect to give an account of what he has done here, who thinks that our affairs stop with the present life and that there is nothing more beyond it—such a person will not care for virtue. How could he, when he expects no reward to be laid up for his labors? Nor will he keep away from wickedness, since he expects no punishment for the evil he has done. Instead, he gives himself over to disordered desires and will rush into every kind of evil. But the person who has persuaded himself about the coming judgment, who keeps that fearful tribunal before his eyes along with the inexorable accounting and the irrefutable verdict, will try in every way to hold fast to self-control and gentleness and the rest of virtue, and to flee licentiousness, insolence, and every other wickedness. And this person will be able with great abundance to stop the mouths of those who accuse God's providence.

For when some people see the gentle and self-controlled, those who live in righteousness, being choked by poverty, mistreated, slandered, scarcely able to obtain necessary food, and often wasting away with long illness and harsh diseases while receiving no protection—and when they see charlatans and defiled men, full of many evils, clothed in wealth, living in luxury, wearing splendid garments, dragging after themselves a great swarm of household servants, admired, enjoying power, and possessing great confidence before the king—then some people accuse God's providence over these things and say: Where is providence in this? Where is just judgment? The self-controlled and gentle person is in evils, while the licentious and corrupt person is in good things. This one is admired, that one is despised. This one enjoys great luxury, that one is in poverty and the worst evils. The person who doubts about the things to come will be silenced and will say nothing at all. But the person who knows how to philosophize about the resurrection will easily check the blasphemy and will say to those who are vexed at such things: Stop sharpening your tongues against the God who made you. Our affairs do not stop with the present life; we are pressing on to another life far longer—or rather, one that has no end. And there, certainly, this poor man who lives with righteousness will receive the rewards for his labors, while the licentious charlatan will pay the penalty for this wickedness and unjust luxury.

last_rejected.why: English hides that this is the objector's interlocutor being silenced, not a general doubter.

last_rejected.why: Present participle 'stopping' obscures that this was completed past action in the earlier discourse.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιστομίζοντες is a standard circumstantial participle; 'stopping' correctly renders ongoing action in context.
